title: JavaScript and the DOM
summary: Load scripts the right way, find and change elements, handle events, and see how the event loop decides when the page updates.
intro: Everything a page does after it loads is JavaScript changing the DOM: a menu that opens, a like button that counts, a list that filters as you type, a form that warns you before it sends. The previous lesson taught the language. This one points it at the page. It covers how scripts load without slowing the page down, how to find elements, how to change them safely, how to run code when people click and type, and how the browser decides when your changes appear on screen. The last part puts it together in a small app, and shows the problem every growing page runs into, which is the reason tools like React exist.

steps.title: How scripts load and run
steps.body:
A script that loads the wrong way either runs before the elements it needs exist, or holds up the whole page while it downloads. Both are common, and both are easy to avoid once you know what the browser does when it meets a `script` element.

## The parser stops for a script

The lesson on how a browser draws a page showed the parser reading HTML from the top and building the DOM, the tree of objects that stands for the page, as it goes. A plain `<script src="app.js">`, called a **classic script**, interrupts that. When the parser reaches it, it stops building, waits for the file to download, runs it, and only then carries on.

That causes two problems. A script in the `head` runs before the browser has read the `body`, so the elements it looks for don't exist yet, and looking for one gives `null`. And while the file downloads, nothing below the `script` element appears on screen. The previous lesson put scripts at the very end of the page to avoid both, which works, but the download can't start until the parser gets there.

## defer and async

Two attributes let the parser keep going while a script downloads:

- `defer` downloads the script alongside the parsing, then runs it once the whole page has been parsed. Deferred scripts run in the order they appear in the HTML. This is the one to use for scripts that work with the page: it starts the download early, and every element exists by the time it runs.
- `async` downloads alongside the parsing too, but runs the script the moment it arrives, pausing the parser if it's still going. Async scripts run in whatever order they finish downloading. That suits scripts that stand alone and don't touch the page, like a visitor counter.

```diagram javascript-and-the-dom-script-loading
Classic scripts stop the parser. defer and async download alongside it, and differ in when they run.
```

In the diagram, each row is the same page. The classic script stops the parser while it downloads and runs. The deferred script downloads during parsing and runs after it. The async script also downloads during parsing, but runs as soon as it's ready, pausing the parser for just as long as it runs.

So the usual place for a script is the `head`, with `defer`: `<script src="app.js" defer></script>`.

## Modules

Bigger programs are split into files, and each file is a **module**: a file that can share some of its names with other files and keep the rest to itself. The page loads one with `type="module"`:

```html
<script type="module" src="main.js"></script>
```

A module shares a name with `export`, and another module uses it with `import`:

```javascript
export function formatKm(km) {
  return `${km} km`;
}
```

That's `format.js`. In `main.js`, `import { formatKm } from "./format.js";` brings `formatKm` in, and the browser downloads `format.js` by itself. The path must start with `./`, `../`, or `/`, like a relative path in a link. A file can also have one `export default`, imported without the curly brackets.

Modules differ from classic scripts in four ways that matter:

- **They're deferred.** A module script waits for the page to be parsed, with no attribute needed.
- **Each has its own scope.** Names made at the top of a module stay in that module unless it exports them. Classic scripts all share one scope, so two of them that both make a `const total` clash, and the second one stops with an error.
- **They're strict.** Modules run in **strict mode**, which turns some old, quiet mistakes into errors, like assigning to a variable that was never made.
- **They need a server.** Open a page from your disk, by double-clicking it, and its modules won't load: the browser's rules for fetching files, from the lesson after this one, don't allow it. Serve the folder, the way you have been with Python's server.

## window and document

Two objects are always there for a script. `window` is the browser tab itself, and it's the **global object**: everything the browser gives your code hangs off it, like `window.innerWidth`, the viewport's width, or `window.setTimeout`. Its properties are global, so you can write `setTimeout` without the `window.` in front.

`document` is the DOM: the page, as objects you can read and change. Everything in the rest of this lesson starts from it. And `console`, which you've been using, hangs off `window` too.

examples.title: A head that loads scripts without blocking
examples.prompt: The usual way to load scripts in a page's head today: the app as a module, and a small stand-alone script with async.
examples.code: Trails near you
examples.explanation: Both scripts sit in the `head`, so the browser finds them early and starts downloading them while it parses the rest of the page. `main.js` is a module, so it's deferred without saying so: it runs after the whole page has been parsed, when the `h1` and everything else exist. `visit-counter.js` is `async`: it runs whenever it arrives, maybe before the `h1` exists, which is fine because it never touches the page. If `main.js` were a classic script, it would need `defer` to behave the same way. Nothing here stops the parser, so the page appears as soon as its HTML and CSS are ready.

examples.title: Importing from another module
examples.prompt: main.js imports two names from format.js. Besides formatKm, from above, format.js exports a const called units, and keeps a third, secret, to itself.
examples.explanation: For this example, `format.js` also has `export const units = "metric";`, and a `const secret` with no `export` in front. The `import` line names the two it wants, in curly brackets, and the path `./format.js` means the file next to `main.js`. Both imported names work like names made in this file. `secret` was never exported, so it doesn't exist here, and `typeof` gives `"undefined"` instead of an error. That's a module's own scope: only what a file exports can be used elsewhere, so two modules can each have a `secret` of their own without clashing.

examples.title: A classic script that runs too early
examples.prompt: early.js is loaded by a plain script element in the page's head, with no defer. The page's h1 comes later, in the body.
examples.output:
null
Uncaught TypeError: Cannot set properties of null (setting 'textContent')
examples.explanation: The parser stopped at the `script` element in the `head` and ran this file straight away, before it had read the `body`. So there's no `h1` in the DOM yet, and `document.querySelector("h1")`, which the next part explains, finds nothing and gives `null`. Setting a property on `null` is the TypeError the previous lesson warned about, here with setting in place of reading. Add `defer` to the `script` element, or make it a module, and the same three lines work: they run after the whole page is parsed, the `h1` is found, and its text changes. When a script works at the end of the body but breaks in the head, this is why.

steps.title: Finding elements
steps.body:
Before you can change something on the page, you need to get hold of it. Every element in the DOM is an object, and finding the right one is usually the first line of any script that works with a page.

## querySelector

`document.querySelector()` takes a **selector**, the same kind you wrote in CSS, and gives back the first element that matches it:

```javascript
const heading = document.querySelector("h1");
const form = document.querySelector("#signup");
const firstCard = document.querySelector(".trail");
const ridge = document.querySelector('[data-id="ridge"]');
```

Anything that works in a stylesheet works here: a tag, `#` for an id, `.` for a class, attribute selectors, and combinators like `nav a`. When nothing matches, it gives back `null`, which is why the TypeError from the previous part is the most common error in browser code. If a script can't find something, check the selector in the Console first: `document.querySelector(".trail")` there shows the element, or `null`.

`document.querySelectorAll()` gives back every match, in the order they come in the page, as a **NodeList**, a list you can loop over with `for...of`, count with `length`, and index like an array, as in `cards[0]`. With no matches, it's an empty list, not `null`. A NodeList isn't a real array, so it lacks `filter` and `map`. `Array.from(cards)` turns it into one when you need them.

You'll also see `document.getElementById("signup")`, an older method that takes an id with no `#`. It does the same job as `querySelector("#signup")`.

## Searching inside an element

`querySelector` and `querySelectorAll` are methods of every element, not just of `document`. Called on an element, they search only inside it:

```javascript
const card = document.querySelector('[data-id="ridge"]');
const title = card.querySelector("h2");
```

That finds the `h2` in that one card, not the first `h2` on the page. Searching from the nearest element that makes sense keeps your code from picking up something elsewhere on the page by accident.

## closest and matches

Searching can go up as well as down. `element.closest(selector)` starts at the element itself and walks up through its parent, its parent's parent, and so on, and gives back the first one that matches, or `null`. It's how you get from a button to the card it belongs to, which you'll do in every list that has buttons in it. `element.matches(selector)` just answers whether this element matches: `true` or `false`.

## Nodes and elements

As the lesson on how a browser draws a page showed, the DOM holds more than elements. Every piece of text is a text node, comments are nodes too, and node is the word for any of them. That includes the spaces and line breaks between your tags: a list written over several lines has text nodes of whitespace between its items.

Most of the time you only want elements, so each way of walking the tree comes in two forms:

| Every node | Elements only |
|---|---|
| `childNodes` | `children` |
| `firstChild` | `firstElementChild` |
| `nextSibling` | `nextElementSibling` |
| `parentNode` | `parentElement` |

Use the elements-only ones unless you're after the text itself. Siblings are elements with the same parent, so `nextElementSibling` is the next item in a list.

## Live and static lists

`querySelectorAll` takes a snapshot: its list stays the same even if the page changes afterwards. That's called **static**. A few older ways of finding things, like `children` and `getElementsByClassName()`, give **live** lists, which update by themselves as elements are added and removed. Live lists surprise people in loops: remove items from a live list while looping over it, and the loop skips some, since the list shrinks under it. Snapshots don't have that problem, which is one reason `querySelectorAll` is the usual choice.

## Finding elements with DevTools

In the Elements panel, click any element, then switch to the Console and type `$0`: it's the element you selected, ready to try methods on. Right-click an element and choose **Copy**, then **Copy selector**, to get a selector for it, though one you write yourself, based on classes or `data-` attributes, survives changes to the page far better.

examples.title: Finding one, then all
examples.prompt: find.js runs with defer on a page with an h1 and three trail cards, each an li with the class trail, a data-id, an h2, and a p.
examples.output:
Trails near you
3
Lake Loop
Ridge Trail
North Loop
12 km, hard
null
examples.explanation: `textContent` is an element's text, which the next part covers. The selector `.trail h2` means an `h2` inside an element with the class `trail`, and `querySelectorAll` finds all three, in page order, so the loop prints each name. The attribute selector finds the card whose `data-id` is `ridge`, and calling `querySelector` on that card finds the `p` inside it alone, not the first `p` on the page. The last line looks for a class no element has, and gets `null`. Asking that `null` for its `textContent` would stop the script, so when an element might not be there, check it with an `if` first.

examples.title: From a button up to its card
examples.prompt: On the same page, each card has a Save button. Starting from the second card's button, the script walks up to the card.
examples.output:
ridge
Ridge Trail
true
false
null
examples.explanation: Index 1 of the NodeList is the second Save button. `closest(".trail")` walks up from it and stops at the `li` with the class `trail`, the button's own card. `card.dataset.id` reads its `data-id` attribute, which the next part explains, and the card's own `h2` gives the trail's name. So from a button alone, you know which trail it's for, which is exactly what you'll need when someone clicks it. `matches` checks the button itself: it has the class `save`, not `trail`. And `closest(".sidebar")` walks all the way up to the top of the page without a match, so it gives `null`.

examples.title: Text nodes between the tags
examples.prompt: The trail list is written over several lines, one card per line in the HTML, with three cards in it.
examples.explanation: The list has three `li` elements, but seven child nodes: the line breaks and spaces before, between, and after the cards are four text nodes, mixed in with the three elements. `children` skips the text and counts the three cards. `firstChild` is the whitespace before the first card, a text node, whose `nodeName` is `#text`. `firstElementChild` skips it and lands on the first `li`, with its name in capitals, the way the DOM reports tag names. From there, `nextElementSibling` steps to the second card, the Ridge Trail. Reach for the element versions by habit, and whitespace in your HTML never trips you up.

steps.title: Changing the page
steps.body:
Once you have an element, you can change what it says, add new elements next to it, switch its styles, and remove it. These are the moves behind every update a page makes, and one of them, if used carelessly, lets attackers run their code on your page. ## textContent and innerHTML `textContent` is all the text inside an element. Assigning to it replaces everything inside with that text: ```javascript heading.textContent = "Trails near you"; ``` The text is only ever text. If it contains ``, the page shows the characters `` rather than making anything bold. `innerHTML` is the element's contents as HTML. Assigning to it makes the browser parse the string as HTML and build new elements from it: ```javascript list.innerHTML = "
  • Lake Loop
  • Ridge Trail
    • "; ``` That's convenient, and dangerous. If any part of the string came from a person, like a comment, a user name, or a search in the address, they can put HTML in it, and the browser will build whatever they wrote. That includes elements that run JavaScript, like an `img` whose `onerror` attribute holds code. Their code then runs in your page, for every visitor who sees it, with access to everything your own code can reach: it can read what's on the page, send requests as the visitor, and change what they see. That attack is called **XSS**, short for cross-site scripting, and it's one of the most common security holes on the web. The rule is simple: use `textContent` for anything with text you didn't write yourself, and build elements with the methods below. Keep `innerHTML` for strings that are entirely your own. ## Making and adding elements `document.createElement("li")` makes a new element that isn't on the page yet. Fill it in, then put it somewhere: - `parent.append(child)` adds it at the end of the parent. It takes several at once, and strings too, which become text. - `parent.prepend(child)` adds it at the start. - `element.before(other)` and `element.after(other)` put something next to an element. - `element.remove()` takes an element off the page. - `parent.replaceChildren(...)` removes everything inside the parent and puts in what you give it. With nothing in the brackets, it just empties the parent. Adding an element that's already on the page moves it, since an element can only be in one place. ## Classes, data, and attributes Keep styles in CSS and use JavaScript to switch classes. `classList` does it: - `element.classList.add("open")` and `element.classList.remove("open")`. - `element.classList.toggle("open")` adds it if missing and removes it if there. With a second argument, `toggle("open", isOpen)`, it adds it when `isOpen` is `true` and removes it when it's `false`. - `element.classList.contains("open")` answers `true` or `false`. Then the CSS for `.open` decides what open looks like, and the design can change without touching the script. `data-` attributes, from the HTML lessons, carry your own information on an element, and `dataset` reads and writes them. `data-id="ridge"` is `element.dataset.id`, and `data-trail-id` is `element.dataset.trailId`: the dashes become camelCase. The values are always strings. Other attributes have matching properties: `img.src`, `a.href`, `input.value`, `button.disabled`, `element.hidden`. There's a difference worth knowing. An **attribute** is what's written in the HTML, read with `getAttribute()` and set with `setAttribute()`. A **property** is the live value on the object right now. For a text field, `getAttribute("value")` is what the HTML said at the start, and `input.value` is what's in the field now, after someone typed. Use the property, unless you specifically want the original. `element.style` sets one style directly, like `element.style.setProperty("--progress", "40%")` for a custom property that the CSS uses. Keep it for values that change all the time. For everything else, a class is easier to read and to override. ## Templates Building a card from ten `createElement` calls gets long. A `template` element holds HTML that the browser parses but never shows: a blueprint for repeated pieces. ```html ``` `template.content.cloneNode(true)` makes a fresh copy of what's inside, with everything nested in it. Fill in the copy's text with `textContent`, then `append` it. The copy is a **DocumentFragment**, a container for nodes that isn't on the page, and appending it moves its contents into place in one go.

examples.title: Building a list from an array
examples.prompt: The page has an empty ul with the class trail-list. The script makes one li for each name in an array.
examples.explanation: Each time round the loop, `createElement` makes a new `li` that isn't on the page yet. `textContent` gives it the trail's name, and `append` adds it to the end of the list, where it appears. After the loop, the list has three children. `outerHTML` is the element itself as HTML, its own tags included, and it shows what the script built: three `li` elements in the `ul`, in the order of the array. This is how most lists on the web are made, from data that arrives as an array. Because the names go in through `textContent`, a name with a `<` in it would show as written, never as HTML.

examples.title: textContent and innerHTML with the same comment
examples.prompt: A comment from a visitor contains HTML. The script puts it in one paragraph with textContent and in another with innerHTML.
examples.explanation: The first paragraph shows the whole comment as text, angle brackets and all, and has no child elements: `textContent` never makes HTML. The second paragraph parses the comment, so it now holds a real `img`. Its `src` is empty, the image fails to load, and the browser runs the code in `onerror`, which prints This code ran!. Here it's only a message, but an attacker's code could do anything your own code can, for every visitor who sees the comment. Put text from people on the page with `textContent`, always, and this whole class of attack can't happen.

examples.title: Cards from a template
examples.prompt: The page has the trail-card template shown above and an empty list. The script makes a card from the template for each trail object.
examples.explanation: Each copy of the template is a fragment holding one new `li`. `dataset.id` sets its `data-id` attribute, and `classList.toggle` with a second argument adds `dogs-allowed` only for trails that allow dogs, so Ridge Trail doesn't get it, while Lake Loop does. The `h2` and the `p` get their text, and `append` moves the card onto the page. The printed HTML keeps the line breaks and spaces from the template, which is harmless. The structure lives in the HTML, where it's easy to read and change, and the script only fills in the values.

steps.title: Events
steps.body:
A page responds to people through **events**: messages the browser sends when something happens, like a click, a key press, typing in a field, a form being sent, or the page finishing loading. Your code asks to be told about the ones it cares about, and the browser calls your function each time one happens.

## Listening for an event

`addEventListener` takes the name of an event and a callback, the function to call, which is known as the **listener** or **handler**:

```javascript
button.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  console.log("Clicked!");
});
```

Every time the button is clicked, the browser calls the function and hands it an **event object** with the details. A few events you'll use most:

| Event | Happens when |
|---|---|
| `click` | an element is clicked, tapped, or pressed with Enter or Space if it's a button |
| `input` | the value of a field changes, on every keystroke |
| `change` | a field's value is settled, like a checkbox ticked or a select chosen |
| `submit` | a form is sent |
| `keydown` | a key is pressed |
| `focusin` and `focusout` | an element gains or loses focus |

Use real `button` elements for things people click. A button gets `click` from the keyboard too, with Enter and Space, and screen readers announce it as a button. A `div` with a click listener gets neither.

## target and currentTarget

The event object's `target` is the element where the event happened, the innermost one. `currentTarget` is the element whose listener is running. They differ when you click something inside the element you're listening on, like an icon inside a button: `target` is the icon, `currentTarget` is the button.

## Capture and bubbling

An event doesn't only happen on its target. It travels through the DOM in two passes, and listeners all along the way get called.

```diagram javascript-and-the-dom-event-flow
A click travels down to its target, then bubbles back up. Listeners on the way are called in that order.
```

In step 1, the **capture** phase, the event travels down from the top, through the `document` and every ancestor of the target. In step 2 it reaches the target itself. In step 3, the **bubbling** phase, it travels back up the same way. Listeners run in the bubbling phase unless you ask for capture with `{ capture: true }`, so most of the time you can think of an event as bubbling up from where it happened.

`event.stopPropagation()` stops the event going any further. It's rarely the right fix, since other code up the tree, like analytics, code that records what visitors do, or a menu that closes when you click elsewhere, may be counting on the event.

## Delegation

Bubbling makes one handy pattern possible. Instead of a listener on every button in a list, put one listener on the list, and work out which button was clicked from `event.target`:

```javascript
list.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
  const button = event.target.closest(".remove");
  if (!button) {
    return;
  }
  button.closest("li").remove();
});
```

That's **event delegation**. `closest` finds the button even when the click landed on something inside it, and the early `return` ignores clicks anywhere else in the list. One listener works for a list of any length, and keeps working for items added later, since they're inside the same list.

## Stopping the browser's own action

Many events come with something the browser does by default: a click on a link follows it, a submit sends the form and loads a new page, a key press types a letter. `event.preventDefault()` cancels that, so your code can do something else instead. The next lesson uses it to send a form without leaving the page.

## Listener options

A third argument holds options:

- `{ once: true }` removes the listener after its first call.
- `{ passive: true }` promises the listener won't call `preventDefault()`. For scrolling and touch events, it lets the browser start scrolling without waiting for your code first, which keeps scrolling smooth.
- `{ signal }` ties the listener to an **AbortController**, an object whose `abort()` method cancels things. Calling `controller.abort()` removes every listener added with its `signal` at once, which is handy when a part of the page closes.

`removeEventListener` also removes a listener, but only when you pass the very same function you added, so keep it in a variable if you'll need to.

## Keys and focus

For `keydown`, `event.key` names the key: `"Enter"`, `"Escape"`, `"ArrowDown"`, or the letter itself. Use it to close a menu on Escape, for example. Focus, from the forms lesson, is which element receives the keyboard right now, like the field you're typing in. `focus` and `blur` fire when an element gains and loses it, but they don't bubble, so for delegation use `focusin` and `focusout`, which do.

## Opening a dialog

The `dialog` element from the lesson on HTML documents is opened from JavaScript, usually in a button's `click` listener. `dialog.showModal()` opens it as a **modal**: it covers the page, nothing behind it can be clicked or reached with Tab until it closes, and Escape closes it. `dialog.close()` closes it from your code, and a form inside it with `method="dialog"` closes it when one of its buttons is pressed, with no script at all.

examples.title: A like button that counts
examples.prompt: The button holds the word Like and a span with the class count. The script counts clicks. Here it was clicked three times, the last time on the number.
examples.output:
click on like, listener on like
click on like, listener on like
click on count, listener on like
examples.explanation: The listener runs once per click, so `likes` goes up each time and the span shows the new number. `likes` lives outside the function, so it keeps its value between clicks: a variable made inside the listener would start again at 0 every time. The printed lines show `target` and `currentTarget`. The first two clicks landed on the button itself, so both are the button. The third landed on the number inside it, so `target` is the span, while `currentTarget` is still the button, whose listener is running. Assigning a number to `textContent` works, since it turns into text.

examples.title: The order listeners run in
examples.prompt: A Save button inside an li inside a ul. Listeners on each, some in the capture phase, print their names. Then the button is clicked once.
examples.output:
document, capture
ul, capture
button, the target
li, bubble
ul, bubble
document, bubble
examples.explanation: The listeners were added in a jumbled order, but they run in the order the event travels. First the capture phase, from the top down: the `document`, then the `ul`. Then the target, the button. Then the bubbling phase, back up: the `li`, the `ul`, and the `document`. The `ul` has two listeners, one for each phase, so it appears twice. Each listener is an arrow function written on one line, with its body after the `=>`. In real code, almost every listener uses the bubbling phase, which is why a listener on a list hears clicks on the buttons inside it.

examples.title: One listener for a whole list
examples.prompt: A list of saved trails, each with a Remove button, and an Add button that adds North Loop to the list. Here North Loop was added, then removed, then Lake Loop was removed.
examples.output:
Removing north
2 left
Removing lake
1 left
examples.explanation: There's one listener on the whole list. When a Remove button is clicked, the click bubbles up to the list, `closest(".remove")` finds the button, and `closest("li")` finds its item, which is removed. A click anywhere else in the list finds no button and returns early. The North Loop item didn't exist when the listener was added, yet its Remove button works, since its clicks bubble up through the same list. A listener on each button would have missed it, unless the Add code remembered to add one. `className` sets the whole `class` attribute, which is fine on a brand new element.

steps.title: The event loop and rendering
steps.body:
A page freezes for a second when you click, an animation stutters, a message you set never seems to show: these come from how the browser shares its time between your code and drawing the page. The rule behind all of them is short, and once you know it, you can predict when your changes will appear.

## One thing at a time

Each page has one main thread, the single line of work from the lesson on how a browser draws a page, where the browser runs your JavaScript and also works out styles, lays out the page, and paints it. One thread means one thing at a time. While your code runs, the browser can't paint, and it can't respond to clicks either. They wait.

When a function calls another, the browser keeps track of where to come back to in the **call stack**: a stack of the functions that are running right now, the newest on top. When a function returns, it comes off the stack, and when the stack is empty, your code is done for the moment.

## Tasks and the event loop

Work arrives as **tasks**: running a script, calling a listener for a click, calling a timer's callback. Tasks that are ready wait in line in the **task queue**. The **event loop** is the browser's routine for working through them, round and round:

```diagram javascript-and-the-dom-event-loop
The event loop: one task, then every microtask, then a frame if one is due, then the next task.
```

1. Take the next task from the queue, and run it until it's finished. Nothing interrupts it.
2. Run every **microtask** that's waiting, explained below.
3. If it's time for a new frame, about 60 times a second, render: run any `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks, then work out styles, lay out, and paint.
4. Go back to step 1.

The most important consequence: the browser only paints between tasks. Change an element's text a thousand times in one function, and the screen only ever shows the last one, once the function has finished.

## Microtasks

A **microtask** is a small job that runs right after the current task, before the browser paints and before any other task. The next lesson meets **promises**, objects that stand for a result that will arrive later, like data from a server. The code that runs when a promise's result arrives runs as a microtask, and `queueMicrotask(callback)` adds one directly. They let code finish off a job before anything else happens.

A timer's callback, by contrast, is a task of its own. `setTimeout(callback, 0)` doesn't run the callback at once: it puts it in the task queue, so it runs after the current task, after every microtask, and possibly after a frame has been painted.

## requestAnimationFrame

`requestAnimationFrame(callback)` asks the browser to call your function just before it paints the next frame. It's the right place for code that moves things on screen frame by frame, since it runs exactly once per frame, at the right moment, and stops when the tab is hidden. Changes made there show in the very frame being painted.

## Long tasks

At 60 frames a second, a frame comes every 16 milliseconds or so. A task that runs much longer holds up everything else: clicks and key presses wait, and nothing new is painted. A task over 50 milliseconds is the long task from the lesson on how a browser draws a page, and the page feels slow. A few seconds of one and the page looks frozen, and the browser may offer to stop the script.

The fixes are to do less, to split the work into smaller tasks so the browser can paint and respond in between, or to move heavy work, like processing a big file, off the main thread with a **Web Worker**, which the next lesson introduces.

## Layout thrashing

Some properties make the browser lay out the page right now, to give you an answer: `offsetHeight`, `offsetWidth`, `getBoundingClientRect()`, and others that measure. Normally, the browser waits and lays out once, before the next paint. But if you change a style and then measure, it has to lay out at once to give a true answer.

Do that in a loop, changing and measuring in turn, and the browser lays out the whole page once per round: that's **layout thrashing**, and it can turn a smooth page slow. The cure is to measure everything first, then change everything, as the last example shows.

examples.title: Which runs first
examples.prompt: A script that sets a timer of zero milliseconds and adds a microtask, printing a line at each step. It was run twice, with the same result both times.
examples.output:
1. script starts
2. script ends
3. microtask: right after this task
4. timer: a new task
examples.explanation: Running the script is one task, and it runs from top to bottom without stopping, so lines 1 and 2 print first, even though the timer and the microtask were set up between them. The timer's delay is 0, but that only means as soon as possible: its callback goes into the task queue, behind the current task. When the script's task ends, the event loop runs every waiting microtask before anything else, so line 3 prints next. Only then does the loop pick up the next task, the timer, and line 4 prints. The order is the same every time, because it follows from the loop's rules, not from how fast anything is.

examples.title: A click that freezes the page
examples.prompt: A button's listener sets a message, then keeps the main thread busy for two seconds before setting another one.
examples.explanation: `Date.now()` is the current time in milliseconds, so the `while` loop runs until two seconds have passed. Click the button and the page freezes: the button doesn't show it was pressed, text can't be selected, and other clicks wait. Working... never appears at all. It's set at the start of the task, but the browser only paints when the task ends, by which time the text is already Done. That's why a loading message must be shown before slow work, with the work in a separate task, like a `fetch` in the next lesson. Real code rarely loops on purpose like this, but a big list sorted or rebuilt in one go can block the thread just the same.

examples.title: Measuring without thrashing
examples.prompt: Two ways to make each card exactly as tall as the tallest card. The first measures and changes in turns, and the second measures everything first.
examples.explanation: In the first loop, each round changes a card's height and then asks for `offsetHeight`. The change makes the old layout out of date, so every measurement forces a fresh layout of the page, once per card. With a hundred cards, that's a hundred layouts in one task. The batched version makes all the changes first, so the first `offsetHeight` lays out once and every later measurement reuses that layout. `Array.from` turns the NodeList into an array so `map` can collect the heights, and `...heights` spreads the array out into separate arguments, since `Math.max` takes numbers, not an array. CSS Grid could line the cards up with no JavaScript, but measuring like this is common in real code.

steps.title: Keeping the page in sync with data
steps.body:
Small scripts change the page directly: a click adds an item, so add an `li`. As a page grows, that falls apart. The same information shows in several places, like a list, a count, and a badge in the header, and every piece of code that changes it has to remember to update all of them. Sooner or later one place gets forgotten, and the page shows two different answers.

## State, and the DOM as a view of it

The way out is to keep the information in one place, in your JavaScript, and treat the page as a picture of it. The information that decides what the page shows is called **state**: the items in a to-do list, which filter is chosen, whether a menu is open. Keep it in variables, usually arrays and objects. Here's a to-do list for a hike, where each item is called a task, a word that has nothing to do with the event loop's tasks from the previous part:

```javascript
const tasks = [
  { id: 1, text: "Pack water", done: false },
  { id: 2, text: "Charge phone", done: true },
];
```

Don't keep state in the DOM, like counting `li` elements to find out how many tasks there are. The DOM is the **view**: it shows the state, and it's rebuilt from it.

## Patching by hand

Updating the page by hand means each handler fixes up every place the state shows:

```diagram javascript-and-the-dom-state-view
One state, three places on the page. The handler updated two and forgot the third.
```

In the diagram, adding a task updates the list and the count, but nobody remembered the tab's title, which also shows the number of tasks. That's the classic bug: each handler is responsible for every place on the page, and the more places and handlers there are, the more chances to miss one.

## One render function

The fix is a **render** function that builds the whole view from the state, every time. Handlers then do two things only: change the state, then call `render()`.

```javascript
function render() {
  list.replaceChildren();
  for (const task of tasks) {
    list.append(makeItem(task));
  }
  const left = tasks.filter((task) => !task.done).length;
  count.textContent = `${left} left to do`;
  document.title = `(${left}) Before the hike`;
}
```

`makeItem` is a function of your own that builds one `li` from one task, the way the template example did. Now there's one place that knows how state becomes page, so no handler can forget anything. Adding a new spot that shows the count means changing `render` and nothing else.

## What rebuilding breaks

Rebuilding everything is simple and correct, but the browser throws away the old elements and makes new ones, and some things live on the old ones:

- **Focus.** Tick a checkbox with the keyboard, the list is rebuilt, and the checkbox you were on is gone, replaced by a new one. Focus falls back to the page, and a keyboard user has to find their place again from the top.
- **Typing and scrolling.** A half-typed field inside the list loses what was typed, and a list that scrolls on its own jumps back to the top.
- **Speed.** Rebuilding a list of thousands of items on every keystroke is slow, which you'll feel as the long tasks from the previous part.

The careful fix is to update only what changed: find the item whose task changed, by its `data-id`, and change just that element, keeping everything else. Doing that by hand for every kind of change is a lot of code.

## Where this leads

That's the problem libraries like React solve. You still write something like `render`, describing the whole page from the state, but the library compares the new picture with the old one and changes only the elements that differ, so focus, typing, and scrolling survive. The lesson on libraries and frameworks, later in this course, looks at what that costs and what it gives you, and Hack University's React course builds whole apps that way. Everything in this lesson is still underneath: React finds elements, changes them, and listens for events with the same DOM you've used here.

First, though, the next lesson connects your pages to servers, with fetch and the browser's other Web APIs.

examples.title: Patching the page by hand
examples.prompt: A form adds tasks to a list. The handler adds the new li to the list, and that's all it does.
examples.explanation: `preventDefault()` stops the form from being sent and the page from reloading, so the handler can deal with it here. `input.value` is what was typed, and `trim()` removes spaces at the ends, so a field of only spaces adds nothing. The new `li` appears in the list, and the field is emptied, ready for the next task. But the count paragraph still says what it said before, since nothing updated it. That's the bug from the diagram, in a few lines. Fixing it here is easy, but every new handler, like one that removes a task or ticks one off, would have to remember the count too, and every other place that shows it.

examples.title: State and a render function
examples.prompt: The same page, built from state. Every handler changes the tasks array, then calls render, which rebuilds the list and the count.
examples.explanation: `tasks` is the state, and `render` is the only code that touches the list and the count. It empties the list, makes a checkbox in a label for each task, and works out how many are left. The submit handler adds a task object, with a new id from `nextId`, and calls `render`. The `change` listener, delegated on the list, reads the ticked box's `data-id`, finds its task with `find`, records whether it's done, and calls `render`. `Number()` is needed, since `dataset` values are strings and the ids are numbers, so `===` would never match. The last line draws the page once at the start. Tick a box with the keyboard, though, and focus is lost, since that box was replaced.

recap:
- Load scripts in the head with defer, or as modules, which are deferred and have their own scope, and serve the folder so modules load.
- querySelector finds the first match or null, querySelectorAll finds all of them, and closest walks up to an ancestor.
- Use textContent for text, createElement and append to build elements, and keep innerHTML for strings you wrote yourself, since it opens the door to XSS.
- Switch classes with classList, read data- attributes with dataset, and prefer properties like value over attributes.
- addEventListener calls your function for each event, events bubble up, and one delegated listener can handle a whole list.
- The browser runs one task at a time, then every microtask, then paints, so long tasks freeze the page.
- Keep state in variables and rebuild the view with one render function, and know that rebuilding loses focus and scroll.
